title: Kegerise v. Susquehanna Township School District
lead: A former superintendent tried to convert defective answers into admissions establishing judgment, but the court allowed correction of the pleadings.

actors.name: Susquehanna Township School District, Carol Karl, Jesse Rawls, Sr., and Mark Sussman

proceedings: Kegerise sought judgment on the pleadings on six counts of her third amended complaint.
District court identified inadequate responses but allowed an amended answer under Rule 15(a)(2).
limits: This February 3, 2016 memorandum did not decide employment merits. Specific exceptions and an unpresented document-response objection limit the ruling. Allegations quoted as examples are not factual findings.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: An employment lawsuit reaches a third amended complaint
sections.cue: Kegerise targets the answer rather than proving discharge merits
paragraphs: Dr. Susan Kegerise alleged that her discharge as superintendent of Susquehanna Township School District violated federal and state law. She sued the district and school-board members Carol Karl, Jesse Rawls, Sr., and Mark Sussman. This ruling did not determine whether those employment allegations were true.

After defendants answered her third amended complaint, she moved under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(c) for judgment on Counts II, III, IV, VIII, IX, and X. She argued that deficient responses under Rule 8(b) should count as admissions and establish entitlement to judgment. Defendants disputed that conclusion and contended, among other things, that legal conclusions required no response. Judge William W. Caldwell addressed that pleading contest, not the legality of her employment treatment.

sections.title: Partial answers leave parts of allegations unresolved
paragraphs: Caldwell explained that an answer must admit or deny allegations. A general denial is proper only if the party can in good faith deny everything. Otherwise, it must identify the denials and admissions, admit true portions of mixed allegations, and deny the rest. A genuine lack of sufficient knowledge acts as a denial. With a required responsive pleading, an allegation other than the damages amount is admitted if not denied.

Paragraph 48 alleged a teacher transfer, Rawls’s intervention against the administration’s decision, and his urging a union president to file a grievance. Defendants admitted the transfer and denied attempted intervention but never answered the union-president allegation. Denying one part did not silently deny the rest. Similar partial responses required correction, with true portions admitted rather than automatically denied. The court excluded paragraph 184 because its count had already been dismissed and found paragraph 93 adequately answered.

sections.title: Calling an assertion legal does not answer it
sections.cue: Claims of ignorance also require reasonable inquiry
paragraphs: Rule 8(b)(6)’s provision for treating allegations as denied when no response is required distinguishes types of pleadings; it does not exempt selected legal allegations inside a complaint that requires an answer. Caldwell accepted that many challenged assertions applied law to facts but required a recognized response. He extended that reasoning to pure law, including an abstract recitation of procedural-due-process elements, without declaring those propositions substantively correct.

Some challenged responses included additional denial grounds. The court found paragraph 102’s extra ground adequate and expressly exempted that response from amendment. It noted paragraph 199’s additional ground without giving it the same express exemption.

Professed lack of knowledge also had to be honest and follow reasonable inquiry. Rawls should know whether he approached a union official or visited schools without notice. Information about an asserted nepotism investigation could reasonably be obtained from district records. If paragraph 30 was too vague, defendants could explain that rather than invent knowledge. Paragraph 50 appeared only for context; its response was not challenged. None of these quoted allegations became a finding that nepotism occurred or an investigation cleared Kegerise.

sections.title: Amendment supplies the remedy
sections.cue: The employment claims remain for litigation
paragraphs: Caldwell found many responses inadequate but allowed amendment under Rule 15(a)(2). In the February 3, 2016 memorandum he stated that an order would require an answer complying with Rule 8(b). He did not deem the disputed allegations admitted and enter Kegerise’s requested judgment.

He also reserved her general criticism of responses saying that documents spoke for themselves. She had identified no specific response for decision on that basis, and defendants said they had also denied her descriptions. The ruling therefore required correction of identified answer defects while leaving the employment merits and that unspecified objection unresolved.
